item.title: Methodist Church looks to move away from compulsory levies
item.description: Members of the Methodist Church of Fiji and Rotuma may no longer be required to pay fixed church levies as the Church plans to move towards voluntary giving and find other ways to support itself financially. item.content:encoded:
Members of the Methodist Church of Fiji and Rotuma may no longer be required to pay fixed church levies as the Church plans to move towards voluntary giving and find other ways to support itself financially.

This is one of several major changes being proposed by the President of the Methodist Church in Fiji, Reverend Dr Semisi Turagavou, as the Church prepares to enter its 2027–2028 period of liberation and reformation.

While addressing the 2026 Annual Conference, Turagavou says for many years, congregations have carried the weight of compulsory levies, where fixed amounts are demanded, tracked and enforced.

He says giving should instead come from the heart and be based on a person's faith, rather than members giving because they fear a members are embarrassed when their names are called out for falling short.

Turagavou says the Church should erase the mentality and practice of the levy system and every division, circuit and church should begin transitioning towards what he calls "heart and faith giving".

He acknowledges this will not happen overnight and will require teaching and trust.

Turagavou says the change must also go hand-in-hand with making divisions, circuits and churches more self-sustaining so they do not continue placing the financial burden on their congregations.

He is calling on individual churches to look at the land, buildings, properties and other opportunities available to them and consider whether they are being properly developed to support the work of the Church.

Turagavou says investments undertaken by the Church headquarters are already generating returns and have allowed national-level levies to be reduced.

He says the ultimate goal should be self-sustaining and self-reliant divisions, circuits and churches where they no longer need to demand money from their congregations and whatever members give is offered freely.

The Church's business arm has also moved ahead with several major investments.

Its first service station was opened at Davuilevu following an investment of about $3.6 million, marking the Church's first venture into the fuel retail industry.

Work is also continuing on a 10-storey commercial complex beside the Reverend John Hunt Building, which Turagavou says is the Church's largest commercial investment to date and is targeted for completion around October this year.

Planning and paperwork are also progressing for a new Methodist Church conference centre, with Turagavou hoping the 2027 Annual Conference can be held there.

Another major change proposed by Dr Turagavou is for every Methodist lay preacher to abstain from smoking from January 2027.

He says there are issues affecting the credibility of lay pastors and preachers, including their appearance, speech, work ethic, relationships, excessive consumption of yaqona and smoking.

Dr Turagavou says lay preachers are messengers of God and people see God through their words and actions .

He says giving up smoking will save money and, more importantly, save lives, adding that Church leaders cannot preach freedom while remaining bound by habits they have not given up.

He says those who preach must live what they preach for the Church's mission to remain effective.

Dr Turagavou is also calling for a change in the practice of presenting and drinking yaqona with ministers and lay preachers immediately after church services.

He says while the practice is deeply rooted in custom, it does not serve the spiritual health of ministers or reflect the discipline expected of their calling.

He says traditions of hospitality and respect should continue, but not at the expense of the wellbeing of those called to lead the Church.

The President is also proposing significant changes to the structure of the Methodist Church, including reducing its number of divisions from 59 to 40.

Turagavou says reducing the number of divisions is part of his vision to strengthen Church operations and its monitoring system.

Under the proposal, assistant superintendent positions would also be created to help with meetings, pastoral activities and the overall operations of the Church.

He is also proposing changes to how the Methodist Church Annual Conference is held.

Turagavou says instead of holding a full conference every year, the Church could consider having a full conference after every two to three years of mini-conferences.

He believes the change could strengthen commitments within Church divisions and save money for Church operations.

There could also be changes to the role of Church headquarters in supporting superintendents.

Dr Turagavou says he hopes the annual stipend of all Methodist Church superintendents can eventually be paid by the Church's head office rather than placing that responsibility on members.

item.title: Lasawa ready to lead Methodist Church through major reforms in 2027
item.description: Reverend Dr Jolami Lasawa will take over the leadership of the Methodist Church in Fiji and Rotuma in 2027 after being elected President-Elect during the Church’s 2026 Annual Conference in Suva. Lasawa will succeed the current President, Reverend Dr Semisi Turagavou.
item.content:encoded:
Reverend Dr Jolami Lasawa will take over the leadership of the Methodist Church in Fiji and Rotuma in 2027 after being elected President-Elect during the Church’s 2026 Annual Conference in Suva.

Lasawa will succeed the current President, Reverend Dr Semisi Turagavou.

Speaking for the first time following his election, Lasawa says he is humbled by the confidence and trust placed in him by the Church and fully accepts the challenge ahead.

He says he will embrace the responsibility with open arms and with God's help.

Lasawa acknowledges that leading the Methodist Church in Fiji comes with significant responsibility but says he and his family are ready to carry it.

He says this is a responsibility that his family and he are prepared to take on as he gets ready to assume the presidency next year.

Lasawa's election comes as the Methodist Church prepares for a period of significant change, with the Church's 2027–2028 focus

Current President Turagavou has outlined a number of proposed reforms for the Church, including moving away from compulsory levies towards voluntary heart and faith giving, making divisions and circuits more financially self-reliant, reducing the number of Church divisions and introducing changes affecting lay preachers.

The Methodist Church says Lasawa's election also comes at an important time as it continues its focus on spiritual renewal, faithful discipleship and service to communities throughout Fiji and beyond.

The Church has congratulated Lasawa and his family and is calling on Methodist members and the wider Christian community to pray for him as he prepares to take over the leadership.

It says prayers are being sought for Lasawa to be given wisdom, courage, humility and strength for the responsibility ahead.

item.title: Makoi residents call for more Police patrols after attempted break-in
item.description: Residents along Vula Street in Makoi are concerned about their safety and are calling for increased police patrols after a man allegedly climbed onto the roof of a house and tried to find a way inside last night. This follows another break-in in the neighbourhood last week.
item.content:encoded:
Residents along Vula Street in Makoi are concerned about their safety and are calling for increased police patrols after a man allegedly climbed onto the roof of a house and tried to find a way inside last night.

This follows another break-in in the neighbourhood last week.

A resident , says the incident happened sometime after 10pm while it was raining heavily.

She says she initially heard noise outside and went around the house switching on the lights in different rooms as she tried to work out where it was coming from.

S he says when she and her grandmother went towards the front of their house and shop, some neighbourhood boys who were already outside alerted them that someone was at the house.

She says the man was on the roof and appeared to be trying to find a way into the house.

The resident says because of the heavy rain, they were unable to immediately check the roof to determine whether the man had left any tools or had attempted to remove anything.

She says the man later jumped from the roof, while some neighbourhood boys jumped over a neighbour's fence into their compound and managed to catch him.

Resident says no one in the household was injured as they were safely inside the house during the incident.

She says neighbours had already contacted Police, who arrived about five minutes later and took the man away.

She says when she later went to give her statement, the man was still at the Police station, adding that he appeared to have been drunk.

She says she has lived in the area for about 25 years and has never experienced anything like this before.

She says she also learnt that there had reportedly been another break-in near the roundabout recently, and is raising concerns as this would be the second such incident in the neighbourhood within a week.

She says residents are now worried about their safety and would like to see increased Police patrols in the area.

She says her family also operates a shop, which adds to their concerns, as they do not know what could have happened if the man had managed to enter the house.

We have contacted Police for further information.
